newsitem.title: USA: Lockheed forming company for non-core units.
newsitem.headline: Lockheed forming company for non-core units.

text.p: Lockheed Martin Corp said Monday it was forming a company that will operate 10 non-core business units as a new independent company.

To be called L3 Communications, the new company will be jointly owned by Lockheed Martin, Lehman Brothers Capital Partners III LP and a management team led by Frank Lanza and Robert LaPenta. Lanza and LaPenta are currently executive vice president and corporate vice preisdent of Lockheed Martin, the company said.

Lockheed Martin said it had signed a memorandum of understanding in which the partnership, which is a merchant banking affiliate of Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc,, will own a 50 percent stake in the new company. Lockheed Martin will own 35 percent and the management team 15 percent.

The proposed transaction is subject to the signing of a mutually acceptable definitive agreement, regulatory approvals and customary conditions and is expected to close by the end of the first quarter, 1997, it said. Terms were not disclosed, pending a final agreement.
Lockheed Martin said the 10 units include its wideband systems in Salt Lake City, communications systems in Camden, N.J.

There are also eight smaller specialized companies that currently compose the products group: Display systems in Atlanta, Ga., advanced recorders in Sarasota, Fla.; conic in San Diego, Calif.; telemetry and instrumentation, also in San Diego; Microcom in Warminster, Pa.; Randtron in Menlo Park, Calif.; Narda-Microwave in Hauppage, N.Y., and Rancho Cardova, Calif.; and Hycor in Woburn, Mass.
It said the 10 units have approximately 4,900 employees and had combined revenues of $650 million in 1996.

Vance Coffman, Lockheed Martin's president and chief operating officer, said the transaction is consistent with the company's intention of shaping its business portfolio to concentrate on core strengths.

With the streamlining, Coffman said the resulting Lockheed Martin organization will reduce overhead costs and compete more effectively in the rapidly changing defense electronics and information markets.
He said that due to the expected growth in these businesses, "no net workforce reduction as a result of this transaction are planned at this time."
